entities.title: Inglewood
entities.summary: Calgary’s oldest historic neighbourhood, packed with red-brick heritage, artisan shops, craft breweries, and river pathways.
entities.description: Established in 1875 alongside Fort Calgary, Inglewood is Calgary’s cultural and heritage cornerstone. 9th Avenue SE features independent record stores, boutique coffee roasters, vintage clothing emporiums, and renowned dining, all framed by the curve of the Bow River and the Inglewood Bird Sanctuary.

sources.name: City of Calgary Heritage & Inglewood BRZ

entities.title: Kensington
entities.summary: An energetic, tree-lined urban village across the river from downtown, centred on 10th Street NW and Kensington Road.
entities.description: Kensington is Calgary’s iconic pedestrian-friendly urban hub. Home to over 250 independent businesses, vibrant patios, indie cinema, and Riley Park, it acts as the primary northwest gateway across the Bow River via the Peace Bridge.

image.alt: Kensington 10th Street NW and Peace Bridge entrance

entities.title: Beltline
entities.summary: Calgary’s vibrant inner-city core, buzzing with high-density dining, 17th Ave retail, historic Central Memorial Park, and public art.
entities.description: Positioned immediately south of the Canadian Pacific mainline and downtown towers, the Beltline is Calgary’s most dense and bustling urban neighborhood. Renowned for 17th Avenue SW (the Red Mile), the annual BUMP festival mural galleries, and Central Memorial Park.

sources.name: Beltline Urban Development & City of Calgary

image.alt: Beltline 17th Avenue SW and Central Memorial Park

entities.title: Bridgeland-Riverside
entities.summary: A sun-drenched escarpment village known for Italian bakeries, Murdock Park panoramic skyline views, and riverside parklets.
entities.description: Nestled between the bluff hills and the north bank of the Bow River, Bridgeland is renowned for its welcoming European café culture along 1st Avenue NE, the scenic 4th Street flyover connection to downtown, and extensive community programming centered at the BRCA hall.

image.alt: Bridgeland 1st Avenue NE and skyline views from Murdoch Park

entities.title: Marda Loop
entities.summary: Southwest Calgary’s favourite creative high street, featuring 33rd Avenue boutiques, cSPACE Marda Loop arts incubator, and lively patios.
entities.description: Taking its name from the historic Marda Theatre and the streetcar turnaround loop, Marda Loop has grown into a bustling pedestrian destination anchored along 33rd and 34th Avenues SW. Cultural life converges at cSPACE King Edward, a heritage sandstone school transformed into studios and weekend farmers markets.

image.alt: Marda Loop 33rd Avenue pedestrian streetscape

entities.title: Bowness
entities.summary: A storied Bow Valley river town incorporated into Calgary, celebrated for Bowness Park lagoon, mature cottonwood groves, and small-town spirit.
entities.description: Once an independent town destination connected by streetcar, Bowness maintains an unmistakable pride of place along the Bow River. Home to Bowness Park’s iconic boat lagoon and winter ice trail, Main Street (Bowness Road) local shops, and direct access to Shouldice Park.

sources.name: Bowness Community Association & City of Calgary

image.alt: Bowness Park lagoon and pathway bridge

entities.title: Ramsay
entities.summary: Hilltop heritage community overlooking the confluence, featuring red-brick alleyways, artisan workshops, and sweeping Stampede Park vistas.
entities.description: Directly east of the Elbow River and south of Inglewood, Ramsay climbs the Scotsman’s Hill escarpment. Renowned for its preserved historic workers’ cottages, active laneway tool shares, independent design studios, and the iconic city panorama from Scotsman’s Hill.

image.alt: Ramsay historic cottage streetscape and skyline ridge

entries.note: Coffee in Kensington, a five-minute walk from the Peace Bridge.

entities.title: A Day Along the Bow
entities.summary: Inglewood to the Peace Bridge on the river pathway: whitewater, an island park, the Central Library and a free skyline view to finish.
entities.description: A flat, paved, free walk west along the Bow River pathway, from the rapids at Harvie Passage to the Peace Bridge, with the confluence, St. Patrick’s Island, the Central Library and Prince’s Island Park on the way. Finish with the climb to the Crescent Heights lookout for the view most postcards use.

sources.name: City of Calgary: pathways and bikeways

image.alt: The Peace Bridge over the Bow River

entities.introduction: The Bow is the reason Calgary is where it is, and the pathway along it is the best free thing in the city. This route walks it east to west, so the downtown skyline grows in front of you all afternoon.
entities.methodology: Walked and timed by CalgaryWatch. Every stop is on or within a few minutes of the paved river pathway, free to visit, and has washrooms or a café close by. Nobody paid to be on this list.

facts.season: Year round. Main pathways are plowed in winter.

stops.name: Pearce Estate Park and Harvie Passage
stops.mapQuery: Pearce Estate Park, Calgary, AB
stops.note: Start where the river is loudest. Harvie Passage replaced the old Calgary weir, long nicknamed the drowning machine, with rapids that paddlers and rafters can run and a channel that lets fish through.
stops.tip: Watch from the bank. The rapids are for experienced paddlers only.

stops.name: Fort Calgary and the confluence
stops.mapQuery: Fort Calgary, 750 9 Ave SE, Calgary, AB
stops.note: The Elbow meets the Bow here, and in 1875 the North-West Mounted Police built the fort the city grew out of. The grounds and the river edge are free to wander.

stops.name: St. Patrick’s Island
stops.mapQuery: St. Patrick’s Island Park, Calgary, AB
stops.note: A whole island park a bridge away from downtown, with a pebble beach, a sledding hill and Bloom, a tall sculpture built from retired city streetlights.
stops.tip: Cross on the George C. King Bridge, the one shaped like a skipping stone.

stops.name: Central Library
stops.mapQuery: Calgary Central Library, 800 3 St SE, Calgary, AB
stops.note: Five minutes off the river and worth the detour. The wooden arch of the entrance frames the CTrain running underneath, and it is free, warm and has the best public washrooms downtown.

stops.name: Prince’s Island Park
stops.mapQuery: Prince’s Island Park, Calgary, AB
stops.note: Downtown’s back garden: lawns, lagoons and the River Café in the middle. In July it fills up for the Calgary Folk Music Festival.
stops.tip: The lagoon side is the quiet side.

stops.name: Peace Bridge
stops.mapQuery: Peace Bridge, Calgary, AB
stops.note: Santiago Calatrava’s red helix, open since 2012 and only for people on foot or on bikes. Cross it slowly; everyone stops for a photo halfway.

stops.name: Crescent Heights lookout
stops.mapQuery: Crescent Road NW lookout, Calgary, AB
stops.note: Climb the McHugh Bluff stairs from Sunnyside to Crescent Road for the classic view back over the river and the whole skyline. Best at sunset.
stops.tip: Sunnyside CTrain station is a short walk back down when you are done.

tips: Bikes and scooters share the pathway. Keep right and say “on your left” when you pass.
In June the river runs high and fast. Stay off the banks and out of the water.
Going one way? Sunnyside station on the Red Line gets you home from the finish.

entities.title: Calgary’s Farmers’ Markets, Big and Small
entities.summary: The two big indoor halls for any week of the year, the old-school weekend market, and the community markets worth planning a Saturday around.
entities.description: Calgary’s markets come in three sizes: the year-round indoor halls, Crossroads with its flea-market corner, and the neighbourhood markets run by community associations. This guide covers each one, what it is good for, and links to the next confirmed date we have for it.

image.alt: Friends making plans together in the city

entities.introduction: Every part of the city has its own market ritual. The big halls will feed you any week of the year; the small community markets are where you meet the grower and end up chatting for ten minutes.
entities.methodology: Every market here is one CalgaryWatch already tracks, with dates checked against the organizer. Each stop links to its listing, so the next date you see is the one we last confirmed, not a guess. Nobody paid to be on this list.

facts.season: Halls year round. Community markets mostly June to October.

stops.name: Calgary Farmers’ Market South
stops.mapQuery: Calgary Farmers’ Market South, 510 77 Ave SE, Calgary, AB
stops.note: The big one. A huge indoor hall of butchers, bakers, produce stalls and lunch counters, open Thursday to Sunday all year.
stops.tip: Go before 11 on Saturdays, or go Thursday and have it to yourself.

stops.name: Calgary Farmers’ Market West
stops.mapQuery: Calgary Farmers’ Market West, 25 Greenbriar Dr NW, Calgary, AB
stops.note: The same idea in a newer, brighter building on the west side. Easy stop on the way out to the mountains.

stops.name: Crossroads Market
stops.mapQuery: Crossroads Market, 1235 26 Ave SE, Calgary, AB
stops.note: Old-school and a bit chaotic, in the best way. Produce and food stalls on one side, antiques and flea-market finds on the other.
stops.tip: Bring cash for the flea-market side.

stops.name: Hillhurst Sunnyside Farmers’ Market
stops.mapQuery: Hillhurst Sunnyside Community Association, 1320 5 Ave NW, Calgary, AB
stops.note: A summer community market run by the neighbourhood, a short walk from Kensington. Small, friendly and very local.

stops.name: Bridgeland-Riverside Farmers’ Market
stops.mapQuery: Bridgeland-Riverside Community Association, 917 Centre Ave NE, Calgary, AB
stops.note: A community-hall market on the hill above the river. Pair it with a walk down to the Bow.

stops.name: Farmers & Makers Market at cSPACE
stops.mapQuery: cSPACE King Edward, 1721 29 Ave SW, Calgary, AB
stops.note: Growers and makers inside a restored sandstone school that is now an arts hub. Come for the market, stay for the building.

stops.name: Dalhousie Harvest Farmers’ Market
stops.mapQuery: 5432 Dalhart Rd NW, Calgary, AB
stops.note: A northwest community market with growers you will not find downtown.

stops.name: Calgary Winter Market
stops.mapQuery: 101 Barclay Parade SW, Calgary, AB
stops.note: When the summer markets pack up, this one keeps a downtown market going through the cold months.

tips: Bakeries sell out first. If bread is the point, go early.
Bring a tote and some cash. Smaller stalls at community markets do not always take cards.
Seasonal markets mostly run June to October. The two big halls carry you through winter.

entities.title: Inglewood & Ramsay on Foot
entities.summary: Calgary’s oldest main street, a record store that has outlasted everything, a bird sanctuary, a warehouse brewery and the best free view of downtown.
entities.description: A day on foot in Inglewood and Ramsay, east of downtown. Start at the fort the city grew from, work along 9 Avenue SE for records and coffee, slip out to the bird sanctuary, and finish on Scotsman’s Hill at sunset with live blues after.

sources.name: City of Calgary: Inglewood Bird Sanctuary

image.alt: The Calgary Tower above downtown at golden hour

entities.introduction: Inglewood calls itself Calgary’s oldest neighbourhood, and 9 Avenue SE still looks the part: low brick storefronts, independent shops and almost no chains. Ramsay sits on the hill next door and has the view.
entities.methodology: Walked by CalgaryWatch. Every stop is independent, local, and open to anyone; the brewery and the bar are 18+ in the evening. Independent places change hours often, so check before you go. Nobody paid to be on this list.

facts.season: Best spring to fall. The sanctuary is open year round.

stops.name: Fort Calgary
stops.mapQuery: Fort Calgary, 750 9 Ave SE, Calgary, AB
stops.note: Where it started: the 1875 police fort at the confluence. Walk the grounds and the river edge, then head east on 9 Avenue.

stops.name: Recordland
stops.mapQuery: Recordland, 1208 9 Ave SE, Calgary, AB
stops.note: Floor-to-ceiling crates of vinyl that have been here for decades. Bring time, not a plan.

stops.name: Rosso Coffee Roasters
stops.mapQuery: Rosso Coffee Roasters, 1402 9 Ave SE, Calgary, AB
stops.note: A Calgary roaster on the main street. Take it to go and keep walking.

stops.name: Inglewood Bird Sanctuary
stops.mapQuery: Inglewood Bird Sanctuary, 2425 9 Ave SE, Calgary, AB
stops.note: A quiet, flat loop through riverside forest where hundreds of bird species have been spotted. Free, and the calmest hour you will spend in the city.
stops.tip: No dogs or bikes inside. Mornings are best for birds.

stops.name: Cold Garden Beverage Company
stops.mapQuery: Cold Garden Beverage Company, 1100 11 St SE, Calgary, AB
stops.note: A big, cheerful warehouse taproom. Grab a table, a pint and a second wind.

stops.name: Scotsman’s Hill
stops.mapQuery: Scotsman’s Hill, Salisbury St SE, Calgary, AB
stops.note: The best free view of downtown, with the Stampede grounds right below you. Come for sunset; during Stampede week people bring chairs for the fireworks.

stops.name: The Blues Can
stops.mapQuery: The Blues Can, 1429 9 Ave SE, Calgary, AB
stops.note: Finish where Inglewood has finished its nights for years: a small room with live blues on stage.
stops.tip: 18+. Check the lineup and any cover charge before you go.

tips: Parking on 9 Avenue fills up on weekends. The 1 bus and the walk from downtown are easier.
Most shops open around 10 or 11; plan the sanctuary for the morning.
Scotsman’s Hill is a residential street. Keep it quiet for the neighbours.

entities.title: Calgary for $0
entities.summary: A whole downtown day that costs nothing, built to work in January: a glass garden, 16 km of skywalks, the city’s best library and a skyline view at the end.
entities.description: A free day in downtown Calgary that works in any weather. Go indoors through the +15 skywalks and Devonian Gardens, out along Stephen Avenue and through Chinatown, and finish on the river and up at the Crescent Heights lookout.

image.alt: Downtown Calgary skyline

entities.introduction: Calgary is expensive enough. This is a full day downtown without paying for a ticket, a museum or parking, and most of it is indoors, so it works at minus twenty as well as in July.
entities.methodology: Picked by CalgaryWatch. Every stop is free to enter, open to the public and reachable on foot or by CTrain. We list what something costs only when it is truly zero. Nobody paid to be on this list.

stops.name: Central Library
stops.mapQuery: Calgary Central Library, 800 3 St SE, Calgary, AB
stops.note: Start somewhere warm and beautiful. Wander all the floors, find a window seat, and if you live here, get a library card: it is free.
stops.tip: The kids’ floor is one of the best free play spaces in the city.

stops.name: Stephen Avenue Walk
stops.mapQuery: Stephen Avenue Walk, 8 Ave SW, Calgary, AB
stops.note: Calgary’s pedestrian main street, lined with sandstone buildings from the early 1900s. Walk it west and look up.

stops.name: Devonian Gardens
stops.mapQuery: Devonian Gardens, 317 7 Ave SW, Calgary, AB
stops.note: A free indoor garden under a glass roof, with thousands of plants, a koi pond and a living wall. The warmest green space in the city in February.

stops.name: The +15 skywalks
stops.mapQuery: Plus 15 skywalk, downtown Calgary, AB
stops.note: About 16 km of enclosed bridges, one floor up, linking a big part of downtown. Follow the +15 signs and cross the core without stepping outside.
stops.tip: Some bridges close in the evening and on weekends. Weekdays are best.

stops.name: Chinatown and Sien Lok Park
stops.mapQuery: Sien Lok Park, Calgary, AB
stops.note: Walk Centre Street into Chinatown, then down to Sien Lok Park on the river. Budget a few dollars if a bakery gets you; that part is optional.

stops.name: Prince’s Island Park and the Peace Bridge
stops.mapQuery: Prince’s Island Park, Calgary, AB
stops.note: Back outside for the river: loop the island, then cross Santiago Calatrava’s red Peace Bridge to Sunnyside.

stops.name: Crescent Heights lookout
stops.mapQuery: Crescent Road NW lookout, Calgary, AB
stops.note: End with the climb up the McHugh Bluff stairs to Crescent Road for the whole skyline at sunset. Still free.

tips: CTrain rides in the downtown free fare zone along 7 Avenue cost nothing. Check Calgary Transit for the current zone.
Kids 12 and under ride Calgary Transit free.
Bring a water bottle. The library and the gardens have fountains.

entities.title: Calgary Chinese Cultural Centre
entities.summary: A Chinatown cultural hub for Chinese arts, language, wellness, recreation and community celebrations throughout the year.
entities.description: The Calgary Chinese Cultural Centre is a charitable non-profit gathering place serving Chinatown, Calgary’s Chinese community and Calgarians more broadly. Its year-round programs span Chinese arts and heritage, Mandarin, calligraphy and painting, music and dance, Tai Chi and Qigong, martial arts, recreation, wellness, and family and senior activities. Current fall 2026 sessions include Wing Chun, Adult Mandarin, Chinese Xie Yi Painting, Table Tennis and beginner Yang Style Tai Chi. Dates and registration can change, so use the Centre’s official programs and events pages for the current schedule.

entities.title: Exhibition – CrossCraft Pattern Systems
entities.summary: CrossCraft Pattern Systems is a research-creation project that explores how traditional craft techniques can be transformed into new visual and structural pattern systems in contemporary design.
entities.description: CrossCraft Pattern Systems is a research-creation project that explores how traditional craft techniques can be transformed into new visual and structural pattern systems in contemporary design. The exhibition presents a series of tufted rugs, each displayed alongside a handmade craft reference piece such as a quilt block or a macramé panel. By pairing these objects, the exhibition shows how the logic within each craft practice can be carried across materials and reinterpreted in another form. At the core of the project is the idea that traditional crafts contain their own systems of repetition, structure, and pattern-making. Each rug in the series draws from the key elements of a specific craft, abstracting those foundations into a bold, graphic textile. When visitors compare the rug to its reference piece, they can clearly see how the design grows out of the underlying craft techniques. This offers an accessible introduction to craft processes and a way to understand how making can serve as a method of inquiry. This is a collaborative project involving researchers and makers from four academic institutions in Ontario and Alberta. The team includes faculty members, researchers, and a graduate student, each with their own craft practice. *Project lead, Steven Pong from Carleton University will be visiting LCR late October, offering a Nickle at Noon talk on October 29th at 12:00pm in Gallery Hall. entities.title: Nickle@Noon – Ash Slemming: Creating Beyond Category
entities.summary: Creating Beyond Category: Building an Independent Creative Practice Through Collaboration, Curiosity, and Community A career in the arts rarely follows a straight line.
entities.description: Creating Beyond Category: Building an Independent Creative Practice Through Collaboration, Curiosity, and Community A career in the arts rarely follows a straight line. Through stories from curated exhibitions, freelance projects, artist collaborations, and unexpected opportunities, Ash Slemming explores how curiosity, community relationships, and a willingness to work across disciplines can become the foundation for an independent creative practice. This talk offers practical insights for emerging artists and creative thinkers exploring career options and finding their own path. Ash will share how they built a career by following a path of curiosity and aligning their goals with their personal values. Ash Slemming is an interdisciplinary creative based in Treaty 7 Southern Alberta working across exhibitions, public programming, writing, design, and community engagement. Through their independent practice, 'Do the Art Thing', they collaborate with artists and organizations locally and internationally to develop projects that foster curiosity, reflection, and meaningful dialogue. Always free. Everyone welcome.

entities.description: Held. Together. is a group exhibition featuring Glenna Cardinal, seth cardinal dodginghorse, Dwayne Martineau, and Amanda McCavour. Plants provide the curatorial point of departure for Held. Together. From this starting point, the exhibition brings together artists whose practices engage differently with questions of relationship, place, and belonging. Attending to the ecological intelligence of grassland species, the exhibition considers reciprocity and care as forces that sustain human and more-than-human life. Situated where the Foothills Fescue and Foothills Parkland ecosystems meet, Guts-ists'i, Wîchîspa Oyade, Moh'kinstsis provides the ecological context for the exhibition. These grasslands and waters have known, held, and sustained the Tsuut'ina, Stoney Nakoda Nations, and the Blackfoot Confederacy since time immemorial. Their enduring relationships with these lands and waters continue to shape understandings of place and community. Beneath the prairie, grasses form intricate networks of roots and relationships that stabilize soil, retain nutrients, and create conditions for other forms of life to flourish. Much of this work is unseen, yet it is fundamental to the health and continuity of the ecosystem. Held. Together. draws on this interconnectedness as a way of thinking about community—not as a collection of separate individuals, but as something continually made and sustained through relationships. The artists approach these questions through distinct materials and forms of attention. Amanda McCavour's textile installations carefully observe and materially reimagine plants. Through Dwayne Martineau's looping video, sustained encounters with land and water become an exercise in close looking and a meditation on the sublimity of nature. Glenna Cardinal's familial images embedded on Pendleton blankets carry stories of kinship, displacement, and belonging, while seth cardinal dodginghorse's depiction of their lost home on hide speaks to family, place, and displacement from traditional lands. Together, the works offer different ways of attending to how relationships shape our experience of place and one another. The plants within Held. Together. function as a way of noticing: drawing attention to relationships that can be overlooked and to the forms of connection and care through which life is sustained. This framework allows the artists' distinct practices to enter into conversation, where each work offers a different way of considering what it means to be held in relation—to land, family, and community.Held. Together. honours the enduring relationships Indigenous Peoples have maintained with these grasslands and waters since time immemorial, while inviting those of us who have settled here to consider how we are situated within these living ecosystems and what responsibilities arise from that relationship.Glenna Cardinal (Saddle Lake Cree Nation member/Tsuut'ina Nation) seth cardinal dodginghorse (Tsuut'ina, Amskapi Pikanii, and Saddle Lake Cree) https://www.sethcardinaldodginghorse.com/ Dwayne Martineau (Frog Lake First Nation, descended from a complex frontier mix of early French, Scottish and Irish settlers, Plains Cree, Métis, and Iroquois) Amanda McCavour (Toronto-based settler artist) With contributions from Holly Anghel in the Window Gallery. entities.title: Exhibition - All Netted Together: Charles Darwin, Alfred Russel Wallace, and the Social Life of a Theory
entities.summary: This exhibition draws upon Libraries and Cultural Resources recently acquired D.
entities.description: This exhibition draws upon Libraries and Cultural Resources recently acquired D. Hall Darwin-Wallace Collection, which brings together over one hundred works by and about Charles Darwin (1809-1882) and Alfred Russel Wallace (1823-1913), the British naturalists who independently formulated the theory of evolution by natural selection in the late 1850s. Highlights include first editions, original Darwin letters, and a rare 1868 photograph of Darwin by Julia Margaret Cameron. The emergence of natural selection, the mechanism by which biological evolution occurs, was among the most momentous and destabilizing scientific events of the nineteenth century. Readers who opened Darwin's On the Origin of Species found themselves confronting a new account of their own origins, one that displaced humanity from the centre of creation and bound every living thing into a single, branching family tree.All Netted Together traces that upheaval through the works that made it possible and the works it provoked: the earlier scientific writing that shaped Darwin and Wallace's thinking, and the critiques, celebrations, and rebuttals that followed. Together, they invite visitors to revisit a theory that changed biology, and our understanding of life on earth, permanently. Curated by Annie Murray and Lulu Petsrosyan Exhibition dates: October 16 - December 12, 2026Nickle Galleries Hours Monday to Friday 9:00-4:00pm Thursday 9:00-8:00pm Saturday 11:00-4:00pm Always free. Everyone welcome.

entities.description: This talk introduces the Soil Memory Atlas, a transdisciplinary research methodology and research-creation practice for reading the social and material histories of place. Blending soil data, cultural archives, and living knowledge, the Atlas traces how human-environment relations accumulate, persist, and transform across time and translates those traces into interactive digital forms and gallery exhibitions. Katherine Lawless is an Assistant Professor of Transdisciplinary Environmental Communication at the University of Calgary and Director of the Relational Ecologies Lab. Her research examines how communities understand and transform their relationships with land, soil, and other ecological systems. Working across environmental communication, cultural geography, and research-creation, she collaborates with scientists, artists, and communities to develop new ways of studying and representing human-environment relations. entities.title: Carter Johnson
entities.summary: Celebrated for his warm stage presence, compelling musical personality, and cutting-edge programming, Canadian pianist Carter Johnson is known for making classical music speak to all kinds of audiences.
entities.description: Celebrated for his warm stage presence, compelling musical personality, and cutting-edge programming, Canadian pianist Carter Johnson is known for making classical music speak to all kinds of audiences. With playing described as "sincere, communicative, and intelligent", "drop-dead gorgeous", and even "the greatest thing since sliced bread" (Gramophone), Johnson's competition laurels include being named the Silver Medalist at the 2025 Honens International Piano Competition, a finalist in the 2025 Van Cliburn Competition—the first Canadian ever to receive this honour—the winner of the Dublin Competition, and the silver laureate of the Gina Bachauer Competition. He is a recipient of the CAG Louis and Susan Meisel Prize. Recent & upcoming performances include appearances with the Toronto Symphony, Montreal Symphony, Calgary Philharmonic, Orchestre Métropolitain, RTE National Symphony, Utah Symphony, and Fort Worth Symphony, as well as at Carnegie Hall, 92nd Street Y, Chan Centre for Performing Arts, and Salle Bourgie. Highlights of Johnson's 2026-2027 season include recital appearances at Carnegie Hall's Weill Recital Hall, Spivey Hall, Merkin Hall, and Wheaton College, a return engagement with the Montréal Symphony Orchestra, and debuts with the Omaha Symphony and Toronto Symphony Orchestra. He makes his TSO debut alongside Angela Hewitt in Mozart's Double Concerto. He has previously appeared with orchestras including the Polish National Radio Symphony, RTÉ National Symphony, Calgary Philharmonic, Utah Symphony, Fort Worth Symphony, Poznań Philharmonic, and Victoria Symphony Orchestras, as well as Orchestre Métropolitain and the Orchestra of the Americas. He has also appeared at festivals including the OSM Virée classique, Festival of the Sound, Ottawa Chamberfest, Miami International Piano Festival, Trasimeno Music Festival, and Festival les Piano Folies du Touquet-Paris-Plage. Trained in elocution, Johnson holds an ATCL with distinction in speech and drama from Trinity College London, and frequently incorporates this skill into his recitals through spoken commentary. His performances of Poulenc's L'histoire de Babar, le petit éléphant, in which he appears as both pianist and narrator, are beloved by audiences of all ages and backgrounds. Alongside the standard concert repertoire, he maintains a strong interest in experimental and interdisciplinary programming; the 2026-2027 season includes his debuts in live improvisation and solo harpsichord. Born on Vancouver Island, Johnson began piano studies at age five with Shelley Roberts, whom he considers one of his most important influences. He later worked with Michelle Mares before completing a Bachelor of Music at the University of British Columbia with Mark Anderson. He earned a Master of Music at the Juilliard School under Joseph Kalichstein and Matti Raekallio, and a Master of Musical Arts at the Yale School of Music with Wei-Yi Yang, where he is currently a Doctor of Musical Arts candidate. He also maintains a close artistic relationship with Angela Hewitt, who has been a significant mentor and chamber music partner since first hearing him perform Bach in Leipzig. entities.description: Aemilia Moser is a Canadian-Austrian coloratura soprano and violinist based in Toronto. She is known for her dynamic stage presence, strong musicianship, and commitment to contemporary music. Her work spans experimental and traditional repertoire, from Schoenberg's Pierrot Lunaire to Massenet's Cendrillon. Recent roles include Ariel (The Tempest Songbook), Despina (Così fan tutte), La Fée (Cendrillon), and La Modista and Minardi (Il capello di paglia di Firenze). Alongside her performance work, Aemilia is deeply engaged in the development of new music. During her master's studies at the University of Toronto, she collaborated closely with student composers to bring two new operas to the stage. She recently completed an artistic residency at the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity, where she workshopped new compositions by Karim Al-Zand. This collaborative and versatile approach extends to her concert work. Aemilia has appeared as a soloist with the Winnipeg Symphony Orchestra, the Chamber Orchestra of Edmonton, and the Alberta Baroque Society, among others. In 2023, she was selected as a young artist with Manitoba Opera's Digital Emerging Artist Program, where she created the short film Sovra il sento. Her concert will feature a selection of contemporary works for voice and piano including the commissioned piece of the 2026 E-Gré Competition, ayimihîtuwin (The Conversation) by J. Alex Young.

entities.summary: EXHIBITION RECEPTION: Deployed: Canadian Army Reservists Overseas, listed by University of Calgary.
entities.description: Join us for a reception to celebrate Founders' Gallery's latest exhibition: Deployed: Canadian Army Reservists Overseas.Oct 29 at 5:30pm - 8pm (Remarks at 6pm)Founders' Gallery (The Military Museums)Refreshments & Cash BarFree ParkingThis new exhibition provides a rare and candid look at the realities faced by Canada's Reserve soldiers when serving abroad. Deployed: Canadian Army Reservists Overseas spans four decades of peacekeeping, training, and war, from the 1970s – 2000s. The exhibition revolves around a feature-length documentary film made by Colonel Michael Vernon (Retired) including interviews with troops and operational footage. Seen alongside weapons and artefacts from the frontlines, augmented with stories of service and sacrifice, the exhibits offer an insider's perspective on how deployed Reserve Forces fulfill the same duties as Regular Forces. Set against today's era of geo-political upheaval and pressures on a rules-based order of international law, Deployed: Canadian Army Reservists Overseas provides a timely look at the critical value of Canada's Reserve Forces during a period of expanded recruitment and rearmament.Deployed: Canadian Army Reservists OverseasFounders' Gallery, The Military Museums Oct 1 - Jan 3, 2027 ABOUT THE FILM MAKER: COLONEL MICHAEL VERNON (RETIRED) Michael (Mike) Vernon was raised in a military family. He studied English literature at Royal Military College and Dalhousie University, and was commissioned in the Regular Force, serving with Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry. After nine years in the army Mike switched to journalism and in 1994 covered the war in Croatia as a freelance reporter, before joining the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC). He then worked as a television news producer and video journalist for Newsworld and CBC TV Calgary. In 2002 Mike reported from the War in Afghanistan, returning in 2010 as a Reserve Force officer with the Calgary Highlanders. In 2011 Mike produced the video documentary Desert Lions: Canadian Forces Mentors in Kandahar, followed in 2017 by Deployed: Canadian Army Reservists Overseas. Mike also taught journalism at Mount Royal University for sixteen years, retiring in 2025. He lives in Comox, BC with his wife Sherri. entities.title: TOUR – Weaving Conflict: Afghan War Carpets at Nickle Galleries
entities.summary: Beginning around 1980, Afghan weavers began incorporating images of fighter jets, guns, and tanks into their carpet designs—likely in response to the arrival of Soviet forces in 1979.
entities.description: Beginning around 1980, Afghan weavers began incorporating images of fighter jets, guns, and tanks into their carpet designs—likely in response to the arrival of Soviet forces in 1979. While the motifs were novel, Afghan War Rugs, as the genre has been named, are related to a long tradition of Persian pictorial carpets. The Nickle's collection allude to, in part, weavers' survival strategies and resilience during the conflicts and turmoil of the last decades of the 20th century. Join Michele Hardy for a behind-the scenes visit to the vault and a look at some remarkable textiles produced between 1980-2007. Hardy is a curator, anthropologist and textile specialist who has worked with the collection for almost two decades. Please note food and drink are not allowed on the tour and you will be asked to check bags and wash hands before entering the vault. As there is no seating in the vault area, participants should expect to stand for about an hour. If you have mobility concerns, or questions, please contact mhardy@ucalgary.ca. In celebration of the Canadian League of Composers 75th Anniversary in 2026, composer and pianist, John Burge presents a solo piano recital of music composed by many of the CLC past presidents. Starting with music by founding President, John Weinzweig, the program proceeds chronologically to current president, Tyler Versluis. The concert opens with a musical land acknowledgement, "Wild Rose," composed by Indigenous-Canadian composer and CLC member, Beverley McKiver, and concludes with a rousing collective singing of O Canada. This all-Canadian concert promises to be an enriching historical, cultural and artistic experience. Dr. John Burge (b. 1961, Dryden, Ontario) grew up in Calgary and holds degrees in Composition and Theory from the University of Toronto (B.Mus. and M.Mus.) and the University of British Columbia (D.M.A.). After 38 years of teaching and administration at Queen's University in Kingston, Ontario, he retired in 2025 as a Professor Emeritus. Although his musical reputation is based largely on his compositions, he did obtain his Associate Diploma in Piano Performance from the Royal Conservatory of Music while in high school and has continued to perform throughout his career. He has composed a large body of chamber and orchestral compositions but is particularly well known for his choral music. His composition, Angels' Voices, for choir and orchestra, received the 2006 Outstanding New Choral Composition Award from the Association of Canadian Choral Conductors and was performed in New York City's Carnegie Hall in 2005. The recording of his work, Flanders Fields Reflections, by Sinfonia Toronto on the Marquis Classics label, received the 2009 Juno Award for the Best Canadian Classical Composition. In addition to Sinfonia Toronto, Burge has been very fortunate to write new works on a regular basis for a number of other ensembles including the Kingston Symphony, the Thirteen Strings of Ottawa and the Hannaford Street Silver Band. Chamber music features prominently in John Burge's recent compositions with the premiere performances of his first string quartet by the Penderecki String Quartet and his first piano quartet by the Ensemble Made in Canada in 2012. A passionate advocate for Canadian music he was a member of the executive of the Canadian League of Composers from 1993-2007, serving as President from 1998-2006. He is currently a member of the SOCAN Foundation board of directors and Chair of the board for the Music at Port Milford Summer Music School and Chamber Music Festival.

entities.summary: Canadian baritone Phillip Addis is best known as the ideal Pelléas of his generation, a role he sang with opera companies and orchestras in Modena, Piacenza, Parma, Luxemburg, Cincinnati, Dresden, Bochum, Hamburg, Paris and London.
entities.description: Canadian baritone Phillip Addis is best known as the ideal Pelléas of his generation, a role he sang with opera companies and orchestras in Modena, Piacenza, Parma, Luxemburg, Cincinnati, Dresden, Bochum, Hamburg, Paris and London. He is as renowned for his Count Almaviva Le Nozze di Figaro whom he has portrayed in over a dozen different productions worldwide. 2025/26 season engagements include Sharpless Madama Butterfly at Calgary Opera, his home company, Messiah in his return to Newfoundland Symphony Orchestra, Count Almaviva at Manitoba Opera and both Messiah and Carmina Burana with Edmonton Symphony Orchestra. Recent season highlights include the title role Don Giovanni, Malatesta Don Pasquale and Marco Gianni Schicci at Calgary Opera, Zurga Les pêcheurs de perles with Vancouver Opera; he made role debuts as Don Alfonso Così fan tutte with Pacific Opera Victoria and as Sharpless with Opéra de Québec; other recent engagements include Count Almaviva at Calgary Opera as well as his first Malatesta at Vancouver Opera. Orchestral engagements took the artist to Calgary Philharmonic (Carmina Burana) and Orchestre Classique De Montréal for Messiah. In 2021 Mr Addis appeared as the Count Le nozze di Figaro at Opéra de Lausanne and Opéra Royal de Versailles. He also starred in the Rai5 live broadcast of the new Barbe&Doucet production of Pelléas et Mélisande from Teatro Regio di Parma. Notable successes in the French repertoire include the title role Werther at l'Opéra de Montréal, as Jaufré L'amour de loin at Festival d'Opéra de Québec and Vlaamse Oper, as Zurga with Vancouver Opera and l'Opéra de Montréal, and as Frère Léon in the award-winning St. François d'Assise with the Yomiuri Nippon Orchestra. Mr. Addis balances his operatic career with extensive concert experience. He was the baritone soloist in Carmina Burana with Toronto Symphony Orchestra, in Beethoven's Ninth Symphony with Canada's National Arts Centre Orchestra, in Britten's War Requiem at Cincinnati May Festival and at the Britten LA/100 Festival, as well as the world premiere of Scott Good's The Sleepers with London Sinfonia. He has appeared with eminent conductors such as Sir John Eliot Gardiner, James Conlon, Yannick Nézet-Séguin, Seiji Ozawa, Kent Nagano, Carlo Rizzi, and Sylvain Cambreling. With a passion for the art song repertoire, Addis has given recitals with his collaborative pianist, Emily Hamper, at l'Opéra National de Paris, the Canadian Opera Company, Brisbane Music Festival, Orford Arts Centre, Vancouver International Song Institute, and Canadian Art Song Project. Now based in Calgary, Emily Hamper is one of Canada's most highly regarded vocal coaches. Her work as opera coach, assistant conductor and répétiteur has taken her across Canada and to the USA and Europe, including Opera Theatre of Saint Louis and Slovak National Theatre. She is currently Head Coach at Calgary Opera. As a collaborator for voice recitals, she has partnered many of Canada's finest singers for such presenters as Zoomer TV, Montreal Symphony Orchestra, Canadian Opera Company, L'Opéra National de Paris and Queensland Music Festival. She is an alumna of UBC, the University of Toronto, and the Merola opera program at San Francisco Opera, and winner of the "Best Collaborative Pianist" Prize at the Eckhardt-Gramatté National Music Competition. Her strong interest in new music led to her engagement as principal coach and ensemble pianist for the world premiere of the new Canadian opera Silence in the summer of 2025. Emily began her career on the music staff at the University of Toronto's Opera Division. She was Music Director of Opera at Wilfrid Laurier University from 2019 - 2022, and for many years a member of the coaching staff at Dolora Zajick's Institute for Young Dramatic Voices. In 2015, she co-founded the Stratford Summer Music Vocal Academy, an élite program for aspiring singers and pianists. With her passion for mentoring and inspiring young artists, Emily is in demand as masterclass teacher and clinician, and works closely with the McPhee Artists at Calgary Opera. entities.title: Nickle@Noon – Visualizing Charles Darwin's Interactions
entities.summary: How do you turn a collection of historical letters, rare books, and biographical details into something people want to explore on a big touch-table screen?
entities.description: How do you turn a collection of historical letters, rare books, and biographical details into something people want to explore on a big touch-table screen? We'll describe the design and development of an interactive touch-table application on Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace, the two naturalists who independently arrived at the theory of natural selection. Built to enrich an exhibit, the application uses visualizations of correspondence, geography, and writing to support the exhibition's central story: that a groundbreaking scientific idea emerged not from a single genius working alone, but through networks of correspondence and scientific community. We'll share our process on how data on a rare book and letter collection became sketches, working prototypes, then a finished interactive tool. John Brosz, PhD is the Data and Visualization Curator at the University of Calgary's Taylor Family Digital Library where he provides data visualization support, collaboration, and training to scholars across campus. John's research expertise lies in information visualization, computer graphics, and human-computer interfaces. Tatiana Losev, PhD is a researcher and consultant on public engagement through data visualization, with work spanning nursing, public health, and participatory design. A former nurse and public health researcher, she designs visual, hands-on ways for public communities, scientists, and decision-makers to explore data together — from public health dashboards built during COVID-19 to community-built data sculptures showing national statistics on public trust in information sources. Based in Calgary and Vancouver, Canada. Everyone welcome. Always free.

entities.title: Taylor Centre Presents Darcy Oake
entities.summary: In a world where everything can be explained, this is one of the few experiences that can't.
entities.description: In a world where everything can be explained, this is one of the few experiences that can't. Darcy Oake brings his full-scale theatrical illusion show to the stage—an electrifying live experience that blends breathtaking visuals, impossible feats, and cinematic storytelling. This is not traditional magic. Objects appear, vanish, and transform in ways that defy logic. People disappear, and reappear inches from where you're sitting. Moments unfold in real time that feel impossible to process—and even harder to forget. Designed to immerse the audience from the first second to the final reveal, the show combines cutting-edge illusions with a stripped-back, modern aesthetic - placing the focus entirely on the impossible. entities.description: Joep Beving's new album Liminal, out March 2026 on Deutsche Grammophon, is a search for renewal. Over the span of 15 pieces, Joep contemplates a relationship with the world in which we listen to nature, move with it, and let it speak through art. In that sense, composing becomes less about control and more about tuning in, about finding harmony between human intention and the larger forces of life. With unique compositions like "Elysium", "When humans do algorhythms" and "Wild Renaissance", Joep invites the listener into that rush of possibility: sounds that embrace the luminous and the fantastical, and take refuge in slower spells of deep contemplation of our place in the universe. Sources of inspiration came in the form of *Wild Renaissance* by Guillaume Logé – a book recommended to Joep by Dutch fashion designer Iris van Herpen. An exhibition by French artist Pierre Huyghe, which Joep visited in Seoul, became another spark. Liminal became in many ways a dance, one teetering between intent and intuition.

entities.summary: Taylor Centre and Calgary Folk Music Festival Present The East Pointers, listed by Mount Royal University.
entities.description: JUNO Award-winners The East Pointers, Tim Chaisson (vocals/fiddle/percussion) and Jake Charron (guitar/keyboards), are innovators within the ever-evolving genre of modern folk, crafting a joy-conjuring, dancefloor-shaking, roof-rattling fusion of folk, pop, and dance music. In the studio, four records have captured the furious energy of their live shows, adding to the legacy of East Coast folk while lighting a path for a new generation of music lovers. Already internationally acknowledged as musical trailblazers, on their newest offering, Schoonertown, released January 23, 2026, The East Pointers have come home. Equal parts origin story and statement of craft, Schoonertown captures the moments that shaped their youth: nights out with the boys, the dizzy romance of first love, sprawling families and small towns, two weeks on in a bleak winter, kitchen parties and vinyl records and tape decks, every mistake, every late night, every long drive, beer and cigarettes and fights, laughing until you can't breathe, ambition rising like a king tide, the piss and vinegar of youth, the sun emerging so bright over the horizon you have to shield your eyes–the devastation and exhilaration of all of it. Since their debut album, Secret Victory, took home the 2017 JUNO Award for Traditional Album of the Year, The East Pointers have cemented their place as a defining voice in contemporary folk music. Their music, streamed millions of times over each month, has been featured on television, film, and broadcast, and their acoustic performances on social media have been shared by the likes of Ed Sheeran and Mumford & Sons. They regularly light up stages across Australia, Japan, the UK, Europe, Mexico, New Zealand, the USA, and Canada, and each fall they bring that energy back home to Prince Edward Island, where they host Goolaholla!, a festival celebrating music, community, and the spirit of the East Coast. Vancouver-based Michaela Slinger is punching above her weight as one of North America's most exciting rising singer-songwriters. Her forthcoming record "Green and Trying" (out Sept 25th 2026) marks a shift toward her self-described "Laurel Canyon era" and features 10 songs that detail delicate moments inside relationships, navigate change, and earnestly ask the question: how does one become a good (or better) person? Michaela's poignant lyricism cuts straight to the heart, and this album is like the part of the dinner party where the food's gone, the wine's low, the wax is dripping from the candles onto the table, and everyone's wrapped up in various intimate conversations-some laughter, some tears, but space for connection with everyone. Green and Trying follows in the footsteps of her last EP THERE'S STiLL TiME YET (2025) via independent Chatty Cathy Records; and This Can't Last Forever (2023) and Panorama (2021) via 604 Records. Michaela has a sync for her song "Everything I Wasn't Looking For" in Netflix's "BET", and has shared stages with Dermont Kennedy, Donovan Woods, Michael Bernard Fitzgerald and more.

entities.summary: Taylor Centre and Calgary Folk Music Festival Presents The Bros. Landreth: Tumbling Wild Tour 2026, listed by Mount Royal University.
entities.description: The Bros. Landreth are two - time JUNO Award winners from Winnipeg, known for their blend of guitar - driven, soulful, blood harmony roots music. The band, the core of which consists of brothers Dave and Joey Landreth, has earned critical acclaim and a dedicated audience for th eir heartfelt songs, inventive musicianship, and powerful performances. From their early days attending their father's gigs as babies ("Mom would tuck us into a bassinet and slide us under the bar tables," says Dave), the brothers have spent a lifetime tou ring rock clubs, theatres, and music festivals across North America, the UK, Europe, and Australia, including stand - out performances at Byron Bay Blues Festival in Australia and Eric Clapton's Crossroads Guitar Festival in Los Angeles. In 2023, a banner ye ar for the band, Joey and Dave became Grammy - winning songwriters when Bonnie Raitt's cover of their song, Made Up Mind (from their first album, Let it Lie), earned the Grammy for Americana Performance of the Year. The recognition was a fitting nod from one of their musical heroes, as their own music draws inspiration from the well - worn records of their childhood — Bonnie Raitt's blues, Little Feat's funky country - rock, Ry Cooder's eclectic instrumentals, Lyle Lovett's twangy traditionalism — culminating in a sound that salutes the past while planting its flag firmly in the present. Drawing on the energy of their recent live shows and a newfound sense of creative purpose, The Bros. Landreth returned to the studio for their fourth full - length album, Dog Ear . This record captures the spontaneous and collaborative spirit of their touring band, which includes drummer Roman Clarke and producer Murray Pulver, and marks a new, more effortless approach to songwriting. The band describes the album as a deeply persona l and emotionally resonant work, exploring themes of family and the quest for stability amidst the itinerant life of a touring musician, and says it's "really about trying to figure out what it means to be a consistent force in the lives of the people you care about." With songs like the title track written for their children, the album captures a raw and focused energy in the studio, featuring a handful of magical first takes and special collaborations with pop vocalist Begonia, keyboardist Glenn Patscha, and a powerful guest vocal performance from their longtime hero, Bonnie Raitt, who appears on two tracks (Knuckles, Half Moon Eyes). The band ultimately hopes, "Maybe something on this record will get stuck in your head, or take root in your heart… Maybe , just maybe it'll work its way into some little useful corner of your life, in the way that songs sometimes can do."

entities.title: Ghazaleh Avarzamani: Churn, Earn, Burn and then Return
entities.summary: Examining familiar objects and settings — playgrounds, board games, sport arenas — Ghazaleh Avarzamani traces the subtle architectures through which power is learned, rehearsed and maintained.
entities.description: Examining familiar objects and settings — playgrounds, board games, sport arenas — Ghazaleh Avarzamani traces the subtle architectures through which power is learned, rehearsed and maintained. What appears playful or ordinary reveals itself as something more insistent: a hostile choreography of rules, conquests and defeats insidiously shaping social and political life. Beneath the surface of games, manuals, fables, and educational references in Avarzamani’s works lie the economic, psychological and ideological structures that govern the ways in which people belong to society.Avarzamani’s installations unfold as spaces that are at once seductive and destabilizing. Familiar forms return altered, carrying a quiet sense of unease. Nursery rhymes, games and instructions no longer function as benign cultural expressions, but as mechanisms through which societies naturalize obedience, hierarchy and collective fantasy. Poetic, sarcastic and politically incisive, her work attends to the paradoxes embedded within educational methodologies, exposing how systems of control often appear in the language of entertainment, participation and progress.Churn, Earn, Burn and then Return extends this inquiry through a seemingly playful environment comprising sculptures, textiles, illustrative images, text, found and archival objects. Yet in this new installation, inspired by the Monopoly game, the stakes gradually emerge as more sombre. Cycles of labour, accumulation, exhaustion and repetition move through the space like rules of a game already in motion before the viewer arrives. Throughout the exhibition, each game token operates as an allegory of hierarchy, assigning value, status and movement. The familiar riding horse is replaced with a sardonic reference to the representation of the Prince of Wales and his horse at the British Empire Exhibition in 1925, where Canada famously presented a life-size butter sculpture of the royal in celebration of imperial power, directly linking the logic of Monopoly to the spectacle of territorial expansion, extraction and the gamification of ownership. Butter recurs throughout the exhibition as both material and metaphor: tied equally to the labour of churning and the volatility of churning markets, where instability, excess and collapse remain in constant circulation.At a moment marked by large-scale political and economic shifts that often leave individuals feeling powerless, Avarzamani’s practice insists on the inherent possibilities of recognition. By making visible the systems that quietly organize daily life, her work opens a space for critical attention, disruption and refusal.Curated by Mona Filip.

entities.summary: A Concrete Jungle Book, listed by Tourism Calgary.
entities.description: Book, Music & Lyrics by Joe SlabeDirected by JP ThibodeauChoreographed by Mpoe MogaleMusical Direction by Joe SlabeIn partnership with Forte Musical Theatre GuildRooted in the spirit of Kipling’s classic while boldly reimagined for today’s world, A Concrete Jungle Book is a contemporary musical originally conceived for StoryBook Theatre’s 40th season. Set within an urban landscape shaped by rules, hierarchies, and survival instincts, the story follows a young protagonist searching for identity, belonging, and family in a city that doesn’t always make space for difference. Featuring a driving modern score and rich ensemble storytelling, the piece offers performers dynamic characters, emotional range, and moments of both grit and heart. At its core, the show asks resonant questions for young people today: who decides where you belong, which rules are worth following, and how do you stay true to yourself while learning to stand together as a community?

entities.description: Kyla Cobbler: Gone Rogue presented by Outback PresentsOne of comedy’s fastest-rising global stars, Kyla Cobbler, is bringing her critically acclaimed debut show Gone Rogue to Canada this fall for her first-ever national tour.After exploding onto the scene with viral social media success—amassing over 250 million video views and a rapidly growing audience of nearly one million followers—Kyla Cobbler has quickly become one of the most in-demand new voices in comedy. Known for her fearless storytelling, razor-sharp crowd work, and unapologetically honest perspective, Kyla delivers a live experience that is electric, unpredictable, and completely unfiltered. Her breakout moment came with a standout appearance on The Tommy Tiernan Show, which propelled her into the national spotlight in Ireland and introduced her to a wider global audience. Since then, her rise on the live circuit has been nothing short of meteoric—selling out major venues including Cork Opera House and Dublin’s 3Olympia Theatre, alongside packed-out runs in London’s Leicester Square Theatre and an extensive, sold-out UK tour.In her debut show Gone Rogue, Kyla covers everything from the chaos of Barcelona dating life to navigating a friend crush and the power plays of a barbeque. Kyla brings fearless honesty, quickfire wit, and a knack for spinning real-life chaos into killer stories. On the live circuit, Kyla’s momentum is undeniable. She sold out Cork Opera House in early 2024, followed by a completely sold-out first Irish tour later that year with her debut show, Gone Rogue. In the spring of 2025 alone, she sold out two nights at Dublin’s 3Olympia Theatre, two nights at Cork Opera House, packed out Leicester Square Theatre in London, and launched her first European headline dates. The second half of the year saw her sell out for her first tour of the UK with a total of 35 shows, and for her debut tour of Australia and New Zealand, Kyla more than doubled the initial amount of shows on sale.Now, Canadian audiences will have the chance to experience the phenomenon live as Kyla embarks on her highly anticipated debut tour across the country. With a fiercely loyal fanbase, explosive stage presence, and a rapidly expanding global profile, Kyla Cobbler is not just a rising star—she’s a force to be reckoned with.

entities.title: Ghazaleh Avarzamani: Of Manual
entities.summary: Ghazaleh Avarzamani: Of Manual, at Contemporary Calgary.
entities.description: Ghazaleh Avarzamani. Of Manual , 2026. Ghazaleh Avarzamani Of Manual June 4—November 8, 2026 Exterior Installation In her layered, multidisciplinary works, Iranian-Canadian artist Ghazaleh Avarzamani examines familiar objects like board games, playgrounds, manuals, and nursery rhymes to uncover the invisible ways in which power dynamics are learned and perpetuated. For Contemporary Calgary’s façade, Avarzamani creates a panoramic image assembling a multitude of tokens and pawns into a cumulative manual where fragments of board-game logic form a single speculative landscape. Borrowing from the visual language of classic strategy games, the composition incorporates heraldic symbols that evoke national borders, territorial identity, and systems of authority. The board becomes a model of society: a controlled arena where movement is regulated, identities are assigned, and outcomes are shaped by rules that often remain hidden to the player. Viewers are invited to consider the implications of selecting pieces and entering the game, confronting through play the fraught idea of land as possession to be disputed, organised, and governed. The replicated icons and grids suggest methods of standardisation and obedience, while emblems of warfare, victory, and prestige point to the rewards attached to participation. Merging playful aesthetics with underlining tenors of control, Of Manual reflects on the subtle ways in which entertainment, competition, and territorial governance intersect, lifting the curtain to open possibilities for resistance and undoing. Of Manual is on view in tandem with Avarzamani’s exhibition Churn, Earn, Burn and then Return , which runs from June 4—November 8, 2026. Curated by Mona Filip. Supported by The City of Calgary’s Downtown In Motion Grant Program. About the Artist Ghazaleh Avarzamani (she/her) Ghazaleh Avarzamani’s research aims at revealing and unsettling the often invisible social hierarchies that govern our lives. Through her practice, she explores the fallacies and inequities in our inherited knowledge and manuals. By creating visual narratives that simultaneously deconstruct and reconstruct time and space, she aims to reconfigure materials to highlight dysfunctionality and failure, utilizing collective human memory and knowledge that is often taken for granted. She reveals the extraordinary about the ordinary, and seeks ways to represent the otherwise taken-for-granted. Avarzamani holds an MFA from Central Saint Martins, London. Her work has been shown across a wide range of international venues, including Hayward Gallery, Delfina Foundation (London, UK - 2025), Dhaka Art Summit (2023), Aga Khan Museum (2021), MOCA Toronto (2021), Toronto Biennial (2022), Calgary Contemporary (2025), Rockefeller Foundation (2024), and Meet Factory (2023), among others. Her work is in private and public collections, including the Art Gallery of Ontario, Google, Rockefeller Centre, Arsenal Contemporary, MOCA Toronto, TD Art Collection and Red Mansion.

entities.title: Adelita Husni Bey: Agency
entities.summary: Agency (2014), film still.
entities.description: Agency (2014), film still. High-definition video, 40’. Courtesy of the artist. Adelita Husni Bey Agency June 4—November 8, 2026 Dome Theatre 2014, Rome, Italy. Thirty-five students at Manara High School take part in a role-playing workshop modelled on a group exercise, derived from a 1970s UK critical civic studies curriculum method. Led by Italian-Libyan artist Adelita Husni Bey, the students are divided into five constituencies – politicians, activists, bankers, journalists, and workers – and asked to engage with pressing issues in contemporary Italian politics, including unemployment, snap elections, and natural disasters. In the months leading up to the workshop, the students met with economists, trade union leaders, journalists, editors, and activists, nurturing a deeper understanding of the responsibilities, challenges, and limitations that colour and contour the roles they chose to play. More than a mere transfer of knowledge, these encounters act as a form of slow initiation. The workshop that follows is not a lesson in governance, but a rehearsal of it: a makeshift society in which competing groups seek to assert influence. Alliances must be constantly made and unmade, and no position holds without being continually defended. Everyone has an agenda, and every agenda is performed, tested, destabilised in real time. The workshop unfolds through various stages. First, the day’s headlines are read from local newspapers; in response to those, the different groups develop strategies in relation to the unfolding of so-called historical events in the game. Then, the journalists prepare a newsreel, after which the different groups award each other “power points” depending on who they believe has retained or maintained power during that round of the game. These points determine the relative influence of each constituency in subsequent rounds, creating a shifting balance of power that structures the workshop as it progresses. Throughout this exercise, power and authority are produced through a rehearsal of collective belief. Political agency flickers, earned and withdrawn in the same breath. It may be won, yet it is constantly questioned; public opinion can (and perhaps must) be shaped. As the workshop progresses, journalists continue to document the unfolding developments, becoming not mere observers, but active participants in the construction of the social reality around them. Information is power, but it also circulates unevenly; and positions of influence are constantly renegotiated. Presented more than a decade after its completion, Husni Bey’s Agency (2014) is a documentation of this workshop, reflecting on the nature of power; the ways in which it manifests and operates; and how it may (or may not) be effectively used. Both disquieting and astute, the work resonates as urgently today as it did at the moment of its making, 12 years ago. Curated by Muriel N. Kahwagi. entities.title: Ghazaleh Avarzamani: Churn, Earn, Burn and then Return
entities.summary: Ghazaleh Avarzamani: Churn, Earn, Burn and then Return, at Contemporary Calgary.
entities.description: Ghazaleh Avarzamani Churn, Earn, Burn and then Return June 4—November 8, 2026 Ring Gallery + Atrium Notice : The butter sculpture at the centre of the exhibition attained its peak decay state over the last couple of weeks, and the decision was made together with the artist to remove it from the gallery. The artist intentionally used butter for this centerpiece to allow the organic material to alter and decompose according to the temperature and humidity conditions in the space. The work offered a way to see power collapse in real time, despite attempts to maintain it, as this precarious monument could not last. Eventually, it was responsibly discarded and replaced with a display documenting its existence and demise. This new phase of the exhibition continues until November 8, 2026. Examining familiar objects and settings — playgrounds, board games, sport arenas — Ghazaleh Avarzamani traces the subtle architectures through which power is learned, rehearsed and maintained. What appears playful or ordinary reveals itself as something more insistent: a hostile choreography of rules, conquests and defeats insidiously shaping social and political life. Beneath the surface of games, manuals, fables, and educational references in Avarzamani’s works lie the economic, psychological and ideological structures that govern the ways in which people belong to society. Avarzamani’s installations unfold as spaces that are at once seductive and destabilizing. Familiar forms return altered, carrying a quiet sense of unease. Nursery rhymes, games and instructions no longer function as benign cultural expressions, but as mechanisms through which societies naturalize obedience, hierarchy and collective fantasy. Poetic, sarcastic and politically incisive, her work attends to the paradoxes embedded within educational methodologies, exposing how systems of control often appear in the language of entertainment, participation and progress. Churn, Earn, Burn and then Return extends this inquiry through a seemingly playful environment comprising sculptures, textiles, illustrative images, text, found and archival objects. Yet in this new installation, inspired by the Monopoly game, the stakes gradually emerge as more sombre. Cycles of labour, accumulation, exhaustion and repetition move through the space like rules of a game already in motion before the viewer arrives. Throughout the exhibition, each game token operates as an allegory of hierarchy, assigning value, status and movement. The familiar riding horse is replaced with a sardonic reference to the representation of the Prince of Wales and his horse at the British Empire Exhibition in 1925, where Canada famously presented a life-size butter sculpture of the royal in celebration of imperial power, directly linking the logic of Monopoly to the spectacle of territorial expansion, extraction and the gamification of ownership. Butter recurs throughout the exhibition as both material and metaphor: tied equally to the labour of churning and the volatility of churning markets, where instability, excess and collapse remain in constant circulation. At a moment marked by large-scale political and economic shifts that often leave individuals feeling powerless, Avarzamani’s practice insists on the inherent possibilities of recognition. By making visible the systems that quietly organize daily life, her work opens a space for critical attention, disruption and refusal. This exhibition acknowledges the conceptual contribution of Ali Ahadi, as part of the artistic collective, Freudian Typo, and his important role in the development of the works presented. Churn, Earn, Burn and then Return runs from June 4—November 8, 2026, and will be on view in tandem with Avarzamani’s exterior installation, Of Manual . Curated by Mona Filip. entities.description: Jane Jin Kaisen. Burial of This Order (still), 2022. Jane Jin Kaisen Burial of This Order September 3, 2026—January 10, 2027 Morris & Ann Dancyger Observatory Gallery Burial of This Order brings together three works by Jane Jin Kaisen that underscore her ongoing interest in ritual, collectivity, capitalist critique, and the possibilities of social and political transgressions. The exhibition centres on Kaisen’s titular video installation (2022), through which the audience is invited to follow a funerary procession gathered to ceremoniously bury a world order built upon hierarchy and division. The social actors called on to perform this duty, including artists, poets and activists, transgress traditional ceremonial practices indicating that this ritualized enactment is a funeral without grievers, assembled to dismantle unlivable structures, rather than lament current conditions. The exhibition’s central work is accompanied by Sorrow Waters This Land (2024) and Dokkaebi (2024). The former focuses on the setting for the procession – a derelict resort on Jeju Island that was abandoned following the IMF financial crisis of the 1990s, now persisting as a crumbling ruin of capitalism. The latter features powerful Dokkaebi deities from Korean folklore, unpredictable tricksters who dance suggestively through the space, haunting or perhaps compelling the procession. The exhibition’s focal film builds towards a moment of revolutionary fervour when the procession refuses to complete their task and instead overthrows and dismantles prevailing power structures so that other narratives and realities can be imagined into being. Articulating their desires for transformation and disruption by way of collective emergence and rebirth, the mourners forsake the ritual burial but hold to their promise of elapsing this world order. entities.description: Curtis Talwst Santiago. A lineup for lineups must be Friday. Always that one barber on the damn phone! Bruh, can you please finish my fade!? , 2022 Curtis Talwst Santiago worlds, worlds, worlds September 17, 2026—January 3, 2027 Flanagan Family Gallery worlds, worlds, worlds explores how stories are held and carried across the vestiges of history and memory. Rooted in a form of world-building where inherited imagination meets critical fabulation¹, the exhibition celebrates polyphonic identities that negotiate different geographies across time, weaving the material, the fragmentary, and the ever-evolving within storytelling. Central to the Contemporary Calgary presentation is a focused survey of Santiago's dioramas. Begun in 2008 and collectively known as the Infinity Series, these intimate works move fluidly between personal memories of Caribbean community life: basement dance parties, the quintessential barbershop, figures dreaming in the grass, and broader collective histories such as migration crises and the rise of territorialism in its many forms. These scenes are portrayed as something precious and deliberately sheltered, worlds that can be held in the palm of a hand, inviting careful observation of details often overlooked. The dioramas are imagined within a scenography of transmission devices comprising horns, pipes, channels, and circuitry. Formed into sinuous volumes, these structures situate the exhibition across broader infrastructures of digital networks, material circulation, and regimes of surveillance capitalism², unfolding as an operative field in which meaning is generated, disrupted, and redirected. Together, they echo longer histories of movement, extraction, and displacement that continue to underwrite contemporary systems of connectivity and control. Made from cardboard, the material language extends Santiago's practice of crafting contained worlds like the jewellery boxes used to hold what is deemed precious before themselves being cast aside. That logic of containment and disposal is activated anew here. Cardboard, typically used to transport and protect objects prior to discard, becomes both vessel and structure, foregrounding the uneven politics of what is preserved, circulated, or rendered disposable. This transference of weight reflects the asymmetries of systemic power and selective memory, where what is amplified is not always what is most necessary to hear or remember. With its visible strata and fragile edges, cardboard retains the imprint of pressure and time, operating simultaneously as surface, structure, and record. This textural sensibility resonates with Santiago's practice as a musician, where attention to rhythm, resonance, and disruption extends into the visual field. Horns and channels recur as devices that broadcast and carry messages, except here they appear to modulate our attention. In this expanded field, perception is not anchored in the visual alone; it is distributed across minor frequencies, subtle registers, and peripheral cues that ask to be heard as much as seen. This exhibition is especially timely within the North American context, a land shaped by the encounters of peoples from the old and new worlds, where histories, stories, and identities are constantly intersecting and evolving. The condition of partial relay runs throughout, meaning formed through relation, interruption, and circulation. Rather than emerging as fixed or complete, stories unfold through fragments, detours, and acts of exchange, revealing how worlds are continually assembled through encounters with others. At a moment when cultural gatekeeping, rigid hierarchies of knowledge, and fear of difference continue to structure public discourse, worlds, worlds, worlds affirms curiosity, exchange, and the will to community as practices of repair and collective imagining. Curated by Kanika Anand. Notes: Saidiya Hartman, “Venus in Two Acts,” Small Axe: A Caribbean Journal of Criticism 12, no. 2 (June 2008): 1–14. Hartman introduces the term “critical fabulation” in relation to the gaps and silences of the historical archive. This program is offered most Saturdays from 1-5 PM throughout the year. Materials and light instruction are provided, along with rotating themes and activities. Our program encourages people of all ages to connect with modern and contemporary art through enjoyable and interactive creative experiences. For October, join us to make: October 3: Miniature woven tapestries October 10: Recycled cardboard collographs October 17: Foam relief prints October 24: NO SESSION October 31: Reductive charcoal ghost drawings In addition to the above activities, there will be both a collage and drawing station available for creative free time during each session. These are drop-in sessions running from 1–5 PM. Come anytime — no registration is required. This program is free with admission. *If you have questions about this workshop, please reach out to Vanessa Lamb, TD Education Program Coordinator at vanessa@contemporarycalgary.com By checking in with us at front desk to participate in this session, you agree to: Follow Contemporary Calgary staff instructions. Treat all staff, participants, and other visitors with respect. Behave in a safe and prudent manner. Participants who do not comply with these rules may be temporarily or permanently suspended from the program. About our Education Facilitators Vanessa Lamb (she/her) TD Education Program Coordinator Vanessa Lamb graduated from the University of Calgary with a Bachelor’s degree in Art History and a minor in Museum and Heritage Studies. She has a deep passion for art, especially the conversations and change it can spark, leading her to have a people-centred approach in her work, and an unending curiosity to learn more. In her career, Vanessa has experience in arts administration, visitor experience, and both designing and implementing public programs, art workshops and elementary school programs. Her curiosity is visible in her own creative practice where she explores different mediums, subject matters and new techniques. Vanessa’s work often explores themes of memory, grief, and identity. When not working, she can be found embroidering, painting or exploring nature. Vicky Xingyu Gu (she/her) TD Education Facilitator Vicky Xingyu Gu is a Chinese animator who holds a BFA in Animation from the Massachusetts College of Art and Design and an MFA in Digital Arts & Animation from the University of Southern California. During her studies, she explored narrative, documentary, and experimental forms of animation. Her works draw inspiration from cultural conflicts, emotional struggles, and societal issues, while experimenting with both digital and traditional media to create layered, hybrid, and provocative forms of storytelling. Since relocating to Calgary, she has become an active participant in the local arts community. She has been teaching various forms of animation with Quickdraw Animation Society and enjoys guiding participants of all ages through creative practices such as drawing, collage, mixed media, and visual storytelling. In her free time, she enjoys cooking and baking, watching animated movies, and playing horror games. Teaghan Fetherstonhaugh (she/her) TD Education Facilitator Teaghan Fetherstonhaugh graduated from the Alberta University of the Arts with a Bachelor of Design, majoring in Illustration and Character Design. She is a digital artist whose practice revolves around celebrating Queer experiences through comics and sequential art. She also loves to explore the stories of strange and wonderful characters in worlds that feel imaginative and nostalgic. Teaghan shares her comics online and has built an audience that resonates with her work and her message.Beyond her personal practice, Teaghan is a passionate facilitator who loves delivering fun and engaging programs to connect with her community. Still early in her career, Teaghan embraces opportunities to learn, grow, and evolve. When she’s not drawing, Teaghan enjoys spending time at home with her cats while reading a good book.
